name: Bandial
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Berndt, Wolfgang. 2003. Description de la phonologie du diola-bandial. Dakar: SIL (Société Internationale de Linguistique), 34 pp. SIL Language & Culture Archives item 60065 (draft, 'ébauche' watermark; CC BY-NC-SA).
catalog_locator: Section 6 'Accent, ton et intonation', p. 33/34 (p. 34); supporting remarks §2.1.3 p. 6, §2.2 p. 6 and §4.2.3 p. 18
catalog_quote: L’accent dynamique existe en bandial, mais il n’est pas distinctif. Il semble que systématiquement l’accent est accompagné par un haussement de la voix. [...] Il y a très peu de mots où l’accent est vraiment ‘fort’ et indispensable, comme pour le verbe [eˈbəɲul] ‘rentrer’ et toutes ces formes conjuguées. Pour la plupart des formes verbales, il semblerait que plusieurs accentuations soient possibles, de même qu’une prononciation ‘monotone’. On peut toutefois constater les tendances suivantes: Une voyelle longue ou une suite de deux voyelles identiques attire l’accent. Le suffixe de négation [-ʊt] rejette en général l’accent. En présence de plusieurs suffixes, l’accent se met plutôt sur la première syllabe du lexème. Lexèmes verbaux CV et CVC: accent sur le lexème. Lexèmes verbaux VC: accent sur le préfixe. Lexèmes verbaux (C)V.CVC: accent sur le préfixe sauf si la dernière séquence VC est formée par le dérivatif [-ɛt]: dans ce cas, celui-ci attire l’accent. Lexèmes verbaux CV.CV: accent sur la première syllabe du lexème sauf si la dernière voyelle est un [ɔ] / [o]. Lexèmes verbaux (C)V.CV.CV: accent sur la première syllabe du lexème. Lexèmes verbaux (C)V.CV.CVC: accents égaux sur la première et la dernière syllabe du lexème; seulement sur la dernière si le mot termine par le dérivatif [-ɛt]. [...] Pour les lexèmes nominaux, l’accent semble plutôt imprévisible.

new_statements.translation: Dynamic accent exists in Bandial, but it is not distinctive. It seems that the accent is systematically accompanied by a raising of the voice. [...] For most verb forms it would seem that several accentuations are possible, as well as a 'monotone' pronunciation. One can nevertheless observe the following tendencies: A long vowel or a sequence of two identical vowels attracts the accent. The negation suffix [-ʊt] generally rejects the accent. When several suffixes are present, the accent goes rather on the first syllable of the lexeme. CV and CVC verb lexemes: accent on the lexeme. VC verb lexemes: accent on the prefix. [...] For nominal lexemes, the accent seems rather unpredictable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive dynamic stress (with raised pitch). In verbs, stress gravitates to the lexical root: monosyllabic C-initial roots carry it, vowel-initial (VC, (C)V.CVC) roots throw it back onto the class/subject prefix, polysyllabic roots take it on their first syllable; long/double vowels attract stress (first mora), derivational -ɛt attracts it, negative -ʊt repels it; longer roots may carry two equal stresses (first and last root syllable). In nouns stress placement is described as unpredictable. Variation between speakers/forms and even monotone realizations are reported.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Transcriptions mark secondary stress (ˌ) in some longer/reduplicated verb forms, and (C)V.CV.CVC verb lexemes are said to bear 'accents égaux' on the first and last root syllables (only the last if the word ends in derivative -ɛt); no general secondary-stress rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent is 'fort et indispensable' in very few words, e.g. [eˈbəɲul] 'rentrer' and its conjugated forms; the expression [ˈnɛɛɣɪ maː] has a higher-pitched [ɪ] not coinciding with the accent; CV.CV verb roots shift stress if the last vowel is ɔ/o; a long consonant does not necessarily attract stress ([ˈɡanːʊ], [ˈfɪlːɪ] initial); nouns unpredictable ([bɪˈsɛ], [ˈasɔm], [alamaˈndɪʝa], [ˈɡəsumaj]).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (inflected verb forms and nouns in isolation, with IPA stress marks); author frames these as tendencies in a preliminary SIL working paper (draft watermark), data collected 2000-2002 from speakers of several Bandial villages (Enampor/Séléki taken as standard).
new_statements.identity_note: Berndt 2003 describes 'diola-bandial' = Gújjolaay Eegimaa / Jóola Banjal (band1340, ISO bqj) as spoken in the ten Mof Avvi villages between Brin and Oussouye, taking Enampor and Séléki speech as the standard; he notes Bandial-village proper has minor lexical/phonetic differences. Watson 2015 and Diandy 2005 concern the Kujireray (Brin) variety, which Glottolog files under band1340 but which its describers treat as a distinct Jóola lect; they are silent on stress anyway.

sources.note: Section 6 'Accent, ton et intonation' (p. 33/34): dynamic accent exists but is not distinctive, accompanied by raised pitch; for most verb forms several accentuations (or monotone delivery) are possible; tendencies: long vowel / double vowel attracts accent, NEG -ʊt rejects it, with several suffixes accent goes on first syllable of the lexeme; shape-by-shape rules for verb lexemes (CV/CVC: on lexeme; VC: on prefix; (C)V.CVC: on prefix unless final VC is derivative -ɛt; CV.CV: first syllable of lexeme unless last V is ɔ/o; etc.); for nominal lexemes accent 'semble plutôt imprévisible'.
